MR. COLDWELI,    REFERENCE TO ARTICLE IN OTTAWA "CITIZEN" OF JUNE 2
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I rise on a question of privilege. On page 1 of the Ottawa Citizen of Saturday, June 2, the following sentences appear:
Then, white-faced, but determined, the Speaker moved the next vote. The opposition could restrain itself no longer. Coldwell, shaking his fist, advanced on the Speaker. "You bloody fool," he shouted above the bedlam.
Mr. Speaker, I wish to say that never in my life anywhere, at any time, in any place, have I used those words to anyone. Earlier above the din I had sought to be heard on privilege. I advanced toward the table and I said: "You are a dictator, Mr. Speaker," and I repeated "dictator" several times. Again, let me say that I have never in my life used the foul language attributed to me.

speakeroldname: Hon. George A. Drew (Leader of the Opposition) moved:
speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
maintopic: MR. DREW    MOTION OF NON-CONFIDENCE IN PRESIDING OFFICER OF THE HOUSE
speechtext:
In view of the unprecedented action of Mr. Speaker in (a) improperly reversing his own decision without notice and without giving any opportunity for discussion; (b) repeatedly refusing to allow members to address the house on occasions when the rules provide that they have the right to be heard; (c) subordinating the rights of the house to the will of the government, this house resolves that it no longer has any confidence in its presiding officer.
He said: Mr. Speaker, this motion is placed before the house with full recognition of the seriousness of the motion itself, and also of the nature of the tragedy that has happened here in this House of Commons.
The Speaker has held the regard, I think I can say without any question the deep affection, of most members of this house. It is with the utmost regret, not only on my own part but I know on the part of others, that a motion of this nature should have become necessary at this time. On the one hand, there is a very real sense of break which has occurred between the Speaker and many
members of this house. On the other is the equally deep regret that the high office of Speaker should be called in question.
I need not remind any hon. member here that the office of Speaker is the cornerstone of our parliamentary structure. That name was first formally recorded in the roles of parliament at Westminster in January 1377. For nearly 600 years the name of Speaker has been associated with the authority and dignity of parliament. There have been times when disputes have arisen; there have been other occasions in other jurisdictions when the position of the Speaker has been challenged and when he has been censured for the conduct that has occurred.
At times, in fact, in days gone by the position of the Speaker was an extremely serious post because of the dangers which resulted from the conduct of that office under certain circumstances. It is a lonely office. In one of the many books dealing with the role of the Speaker he has been described as the loneliest man in the house. I do not think there is an hon. member on either side of this house who is not extremely sympathetic with the severe demands which are imposed day by day upon the Speaker, whoever he may be, to rule even without anticipation of what will arise and to rule in a manner which will be acceptable to the members.
I do not think that any hon. member at any time is likely to raise serious issue about a mistake which may be made in the haste of debate and with the infinite variety of possible resolutions, points of order, questions of privilege and other matters which may come before the Speaker for his decision. It would not be upon a question of any mere mistake that the indignation of hon. members of this house would be aroused. Most certainly this motion would not be before the house at this time if it were not for the fact that the continuing confidence in the office of Speaker and the continuing confidence in the present Speaker had been challenged by events of the past few days.
When a statement is made that the rights of parliament are at issue I think it should always be remembered that it is not the rights of the individual members here as individuals which are of importance. What is important is that this is the place where the nation's business is conducted and that what happens here deeply affects the life, the future and the happiness of every Canadian.
(644

House of Commons
We use the words "House of Commons" very often without pausing to reflect upon what those words mean. After all, it is the House of Commons with which we are now concerned. The other branch of parliament is not affected by the discussions here today except to the extent that each one of the members of that other place also has a deep concern about what happens here. The word "Commons" means the people. This is the house of the people.
Sitting on both sides of this house and on both sides of the Speaker are representatives of every constituency of Canada. Collectively, those of us who meet in this chamber represent all Canadians. That is our responsibility; that is our duty. Our rights are important only to the extent that those rights represent the rights of the people themselves. If the traditional rights of the members of this house are debased, limited or arbitrarily curtailed in any way, it is not our rights that are of concern. What is vitally important is that in that curtailment of rights there is a limitation of the rights of the people themselves.
The freedom that we have here to shape and guide legislation, no matter on which side of the house we may sit, is part of the very freedom which we cherish here in his country of ours. It is here in the House of Commons, to which all the people of Canada must look for just laws properly considered and properly made, that Canadians in every part of Canada must look for the greater part of their freedom and for the assurance of that type of government which will be in itself an expression of the freedom which has come down to us through so many generations of sacrifice and of tremendous effort.
It is with that thought that I submit that we should discuss what has taken place and that we should place before this house the problems which now confront us. The ceremony we witness every day at the opening of the house symbolizes the long historic background of the authority, position and tradition of the Speaker. The mace, which is placed upon the table when the Speaker occupies the chair, is an expression of all the great and honourable things wrapped up in this high office which means as much to every one of us as it does to the occupant of the chair himself. I repeat again, that system was not designed for the advantage or convenience of the members of parliament. It was designed for the protection of the freedom of the people of Canada.
What has happened here is something which goes to the very roots of our free institutions. It is something which could affect, and gravely affect, the rights, the freedom and the happiness of Canadians not only for
fMr. Drew.]
generations but for centuries to come. We all know that we follow the traditions of Westminster and it is, therefore, of importance to us when we examine the position of Speaker that we should recall the history of that office at Westminster, and we should remember that the position of Speaker in the British parliament, before we had any parliament in Canada, had come to represent an institution unique in the annals of parliamentary government. In fact, the independence of the Speaker, as it has been established over long years at Westminster, grew out of the fight between the crown and the members of parliament in the reign of the Stuarts.
Some may wonder at times why we go through the rather cumbersome procedure by which parliament is opened and also why we see the mace removed from the table when the Speaker leaves the chair and placed below the table when the chairman of the committee of the house proceeds to take over. This practice stems from the fight through the Long Parliament in the time of Charles I. The members of parliament suspected that the Speaker was the King's man, and in point of fact they had good reason for entertaining such suspicion. Therefore, when money bills were before the house these assumed special significance. They refused to discuss money matters until the Speaker had left the chair and one of their own members could become chairman of the committee. It was out of that simple and historic fact that this practice and this tradition grew. It has developed as part of their tradition in Britain that the Speaker is not in any sense beholden to the government for his appointment or his continuance in office. We know that there is a different practice there. However, the rules and the traditions are mainly the same. Our own are set out at some length in Beauchesne's, third edition, at pages 52 and 53. I quote paragraphs 105 and 106:
105.	The presiding officer, though entitled on all occasions to be treated with the greatest attention and respect by the individual members, because the power, and dignity, and honour of the assembly are officially embodied in his person, is yet but the servant of the house. He is selected and appointed to the trust of presiding officer, in the confidence and upon the supposition of the conformity of his will to that of the assembly.
106.	The Speaker's duty as the official mouthpiece of the house is extremely well expressed in a few words by Mr. Speaker Lenthall, who, when that ill-advised monarch, Charles I came into House of Commons, and having taken the Speaker's chair, asked him "whether any of the five members that he came to apprehend were in the House, whether he saw any of them, and where they were?"-made this answer:-"May it please your majesty, I have neither eyes to see, nor tongue to speak, in this place but as the House is pleased to direct me, whose servant I am here,

and humbly beg your majesty's pardon that I cannot give any other answer than this, to what your majesty is pleased to demand of me."
There are three branches of government here, in Britain or in the other nations with a similar parliamentary form. If the Speaker of the Canadian House of Commons or of any other house of commons under our traditions is in any way subservient or beholden to the government, the situation is not in principle different from that which the members of the Commons in England faced when the Speaker was beholden to the King. When you, Mr. Speaker, assumed your office on November 12, 1953 you expressed what we all believe to be the true function of impartiality on the part of the Speaker of this house. These were your words as recorded in Hansard of November 12, 1953 at page 3:
The honour which is being bestowed upon me is high indeed, but greater still are the responsibilities. I beseech Divine Providence to grant me all the help necessary for the fulfilment of my duties, in accordance with our noble traditions.
My dear colleagues, it is my duty to maintain decorum and order in debate, to preserve our traditions, privileges, liberties, usages and customs and, in particular, to exercise impartiality and fairness and protect the rights of every individual member. My experience as Deputy Speaker has amply shown me that only with your advice, counsel and co-operation can I succeed in my new task. I shall, I assure you, strive to deserve your effective support, and endeavour at all times to prove myself worthy of your trust.
It is, I believe, true to say that the eyes of other nations, more than ever before, are turned towards Canada. Therefore, I realize that the dignity of this high office and the reputation of our parliament must be most carefully safeguarded, and I shall govern myself accordingly.
I pray to Divine Providence for all assistance necessary so that I shall be able to fulfil my duties in a manner that will do justice to you and this house, whose servant I am.
I said that we have held the Speaker in respect and affection. We echoed, in our own hearts and minds, those words which the Speaker uttered at the time he took this office. It would have been our desire, the earnest desire of every one of us, that the relationship which existed for so long had continued unimpaired. It would not be possible for anyone to pretend that it has been only in these few days that questioning has arisen, and that uncertainty has beclouded that relationship which we desired, just as much as did the Speaker himself.
During this present session it must have been recognized that there has been a steady deterioration in the relationship of the occupant of that high office and many of the members in this house. I should like to emphasize that long before there was any open criticism in this house there was widespread
House of Commons
criticism in the press of the conduct of the Speaker in the performance of his duties. That was not good for Canada; that was not good for the people of Canada whose servants we all are. It could have been overcome. Even though the criticism had raised some questioning, it could have been overcome if the Speaker had listened to the advice which was being given to him outside the house as well as inside this house.
Unfortunately for all of us the criticism emerged openly in the house during the debate on what we have come to know as the pipe-line bill. It came to a head last week. Hansard records several expressions of that criticism on earlier occasions, but it was during the last two days of the past week that all the criticism was brought into focus by events which every member in this house must greatly deplore. I know that for all of us the last two days and the past week are days we would like to erase from our memories, erase from our hearts, erase from the records that are kept of the proceedings in this house. But, unhappily, that cannot be.
Therefore, it becomes necessary to review what did take place and to consider what our position is in relation to those events. On Thursday night the hon. member for Nanaimo (Mr. Cameron) raised a question of privilege shortly after nine o'clock. He spoke of two letters which had appeared in the Ottawa Journal. He was given permission to read those letters. It was open to the Speaker at that time to rule that a question of privilege sufficiently important to be discussed in that way had not been raised. That he did not do. On the contrary, the Speaker found that there had been a question of privilege. In fact, he aided in the drafting of a subsequent resolution which came before the house on Thursday night.
So that the words may appear in their context with what I am saying now, I would recall that on page 4529 of Hansard these words of the Speaker and the hon. member for Nanaimo appear:

Then at that point a debate proceeded on the motion which had been presented.
Now, Mr. Speaker, that situation was where we left off on Thursday night. I rose to speak and had spoken for a short time when the house adjourned at ten o'clock on Thursday night. Then we met on Friday morning at eleven o'clock, as recorded in Hansard at page 4537. We find that the very opening words of the record are as follows:
On the order:
Resuming the adjourned debate on the motion of Mr. Cameron (Nanaimo), that the statements in the Ottawa Journal of May 30 and May 31 are derogatory of the dignity of parliament and deserving of the censure of this house.
Hon. George A. Drew (Leader of the Opposition) [DOT] Mr. Speaker-
I had then risen to speak continuing the debate which had started the night before. Mr. Speaker then rose and this is what he said as recorded in Hansard;

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
maintopic: MR. DREW    MOTION OF NON-CONFIDENCE IN PRESIDING OFFICER OF THE HOUSE
speechtext:
Usually the deputy clerk reads the order, but I rise at this moment in order to deal with this order which appears under "Motions" as follows:
Resuming the adjourned debate on the motion of Mr. Cameron (Nanaimo), that the statements in the Ottawa Journal of May 30 and 31 are derogatory of the dignity of parliament and deserving of the censure of this house.
I have read carefully the articles complained of and I have come to the conclusion that because of the unprecedented circumstances surrounding this pipe-line debate and because of the remarks that were made in this house by members themselves, it was and it is impossible, if we are to consider freedom of the press as we should, to take these two articles as being breaches of our privileges. It is my opinion that if it had not been for some of the insinuations or attacks directed perhaps to one another or the Chair or to the occupants of the chair, these articles may not have been written. I think we should settle our problems among ourselves and that those who outside of this house, either in editorial 
comment or by letters to the editor, write what I consider to be-and this is the case of these two articles-comments which do not go beyond the bounds of unfairness, I think they should be allowed. Therefore, I rule the motion made by the hon. member for Nanaimo out of order. Do hon. members wish to appeal?
Mr. Speaker, that was an unprecedented action. No one on the government side of the house had challenged this motion when it was presented on Thursday night. The debate had proceeded without any challenge from anyone. The Speaker made some point on Friday of the fact that as he is the servant of the house it is the house which must decide. The house had decided on Thursday night by its acceptance of the motion without any question being raised that this was a matter that was to be taken under their consideration. It had become seized of the issue raised in that motion. The merits of the motion, until some new motion had been presented, were not in question before the Speaker. It was in the hands of the hon. members of this house. The Speaker had not only accepted but had guided the framing of the resolution which introduced this debate. There is no precedent of any kind in this house or elsewhere for such action as was taken. Not only was there no motion but there had not even been a question raised in the house about the propriety of the course that had been followed on Thursday night, nor as to the propriety of proceeding in the usual way with that debate.
Under those circumstances I submit it was not the Speaker's right to withdraw this matter from the house. The supreme authority to which he referred on Friday had accepted that motion. It could only have been withdrawn properly by a decision of the house itself upon some other motion properly presented. The Speaker could not have done that; the Speaker cannot present a motion. Whether or not the motion would have been in order, the government might have presented a motion and it might have been debated. It certainly should have been debated if decisions made the night before were to be reversed.
One of the most serious aspects of this strange course was that when I attempted, as did many other hon. members, to be heard in regard to this matter on a point of order the Speaker refused to hear a word from any member in regard to this completely strange device which had been employed or which was then under consideration. At the moment the Speaker called the vote without permitting any point of order to be raised or any discussion whatever on the proceedings which were taking place, at that moment confidence in the Speaker disappeared in the minds of many members of this house.

Then, as though this were not enough in itself, as though this were not defilement of our rules sufficient for one day, the Speaker after the vote on that decision had been taken announced that he found he had made a mistake in the ruling he had made about 5.15 p.m. the day before and for that reason all subsequent proceedings should be declared a nullity. Mr. Speaker, there can be no precedent for any such course. This is what the Speaker said, as recorded on page 4539 of Hansard:
I said earlier that I am prepared to take full responsibility before this house and before the country for what I am doing. I consider-and I have thought very seriously about this-that yesterday around 5.15, when I was called back to the chair for the purpose of receiving the chairman's report, I made a very serious mistake in allowing the point of order and the other dilatory motions; and I feel that the house should not suffer any prejudice or detriment on my account. I want to say this to hon. members-it has been said very often-the rules of this house are devised in order to protect the minorities; yes, they are. But I will add the counterpart to that. I will say-and the authorities support me in this- that the rules of this house are devised to protect minorities against the oppression of the majority and the majority against obstruction by the minority.
Now', the house is master of its own rules and it is my right to submit a matter to the house. I intend at the moment to submit to the house that, in my view, the house should revert to the position where it was yesterday when I was brought back to the chair to receive the chairman's report at 5.15. I submit to the house that the intervening proceedings should not be superseded, and it is up to the house to decide as to the situation which
I	take at the moment.
It is difficult to read those words again and realize that they were in fact uttered by a Speaker of this house. There is no precedent for any such reference to a statement of that kind. There is no precedent for the Speaker saying, "I made a mistake some time ago and because I made that mistake everything that has happened in the intervening period is a nullity." On earlier occasions, perhaps unnecessarily, the Speaker has referred to times some distance back when in his opinion on later reflection he felt that he had made a mistake. If this practice were to be permitted, then if the Speaker found that on January 11, the day after this house opened, he had made a mistake it would be appropriate for him to declare that everything which had happened since then would be a nullity and that we should wipe out every-think that had taken place. There is no difference in principle between saying that everything that has happened since 5.15 p.m. yesterday will be wiped out and saying that everything that has happened since January
II	will be wiped out.
What might have been more appropriate still, if in fact such a strange procedure as
House of Commons
this were ever accepted as part of our proceedings in this house, would have been for the Speaker to have gone back to a week ago Friday because there might well have been some consideration of the strange decisions which were made on that day.
In order to test the propriety of the course which was undertaken at that time, just let me submit it to one proof. The Speaker said that it is for the house to decide. What he meant by that of course was that it is for the majority to decide. I have been in different legislative bodies and I have been on the government side as well as on the opposition side. I have asserted strongly the rights of the opposition and I hope I am just as fully aware of and just as ready to concede the rights and the duties of the government. When the Speaker declares in his oath that he is the servant of the house he is declaring that he is not merely the servant of the majority but that he is the servant of all members. That is the bedrock upon which respect for our parliamentary system rests.
When the Speaker said that the house should not suffer because of his mistakes, let us consider if he was not actually saying "the government must not suffer in its arbitrary course by what I do." That was what he really meant. That is the only interpretation that can be placed upon the words. That was the effect because the Speaker was not prepared to listen to a single argument as to why this course was not proper. Members on the opposition side who were affected by this course had no opportunity to say why this was so improper. I ask the Prime Minister (Mr. St. Laurent), I ask members supporting the government, what they would say if the Speaker picked up something which had been adverse to the opposition say a week before and then had said, "in spite of all the government business that has been done I am not going to let the opposition suffer by my mistake and am going to declare as a nullity all that has taken place."

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
maintopic: MR. DREW    MOTION OF NON-CONFIDENCE IN PRESIDING OFFICER OF THE HOUSE
speechtext:
I do not want to intervene in any way in the presentation of the hon. Leader of the Opposition (Mr. Drew), but I know he wants to be fair. It strikes me that when he puts forward the contention that when I said that the intervening proceedings should not be superseded I meant by that that all that had taken place from 5.15 on Thursday until Friday should be declared a nullity. I see that there is a serious misunderstanding of what I said or intended to say. By "intervening proceedings", as mentioned on page 4540, were meant the proceedings which appeared on the order paper as being first readings of Senate public bills,

House of Commons
government notices of motions. At the time I was trying to bring the house back to government order No. 2 on Friday and I wanted to do it before first readings of Senate public bills and government notices of motions were taken. I did not want these orders to be superseded by the course of action that I was tasting. Then the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre (Mr. Knowles) said, "No, let us go to first readings of Senate public bills and government notices of motions, and then when we reach orders of the day the matter can be brought up." But I want to say that it was not my intention to say that the proceedings that had taken place on Thursday should be declared a nullity.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
maintopic: MR. DREW    MOTION OF NON-CONFIDENCE IN PRESIDING OFFICER OF THE HOUSE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I submit that what was said is open to no other interpretation. The words referred to what happened at 5.15. These are the words that are recorded at page 4540 of Hansard:
I submit to the house that the intervening proceedings should not be superseded . . .
That means that for all practical purposes they become a nullity. We were then carried back by that extraordinary device to the position in which we were at 5.15. I do not believe that any word that I have said in any way stretches the effect of what took place at that time. I submit again that in this case, as in the other, there was no precedent for what occurred.
Whatever the intention may have been, and it is not for us to interpret intentions, the result certainly was not open to question. By that advice, upon which there was allowed no comment and no debate to show what a dangerous precedent this would establish, the way was clear for an immediate presentation of a closure motion which the government wished to have placed before this house. Whatever the intention may have been, whatever the motives were, the Speaker in that act subordinated the rights, the traditions and the practices of parliament to the will of the government. It is almost unthinkable that at such a moment, and with something so strange and new placed before the members here, the Speaker would not hear a word, to protect himself, as to why he should not do this. He declared when he became the Speaker that he sought the advice of parliament. I know that on that occasion he did not mean to suggest, and did not suggest, that he was seeking alone the advice of the government and its supporters. I am sure he meant that he sought the advice of all members. One of the reasons members are permitted to rise on points of order is so that the Speaker may have advice from every

part of the house on questions set up before the house. That adds to the seriousness of all that has occurred.
If there were any justification for this course, then I submit again that it would be equally proper to follow that course in relation to some event a week earlier, a month earlier or even longer. The very fact that this would be the natural result, in itself, indicates the seriousness of what has been done. I repeat, need there be any doubt about what the government would have done if the Speaker had followed such a course and had said, as he might well have said with equal validity, that he had made a serious mistake on the previous Friday, when events occurred which are equally distasteful to the memories of every one of us? If any question the indignation expressed by the members of the opposition, just let them ask themselves what the indignation of the government would have been if the Speaker had followed the same course and it affected them as we were affected by these proceedings. It is not difficult to imagine the indignation that would have been aroused. The very suggestion of that in itself deals with the question as to whether there conceivably could be justification for this course. It was indeed black Friday for this house and for the people of Canada. The damage that was done cannot be undone.
The government cannot divorce itself from the tragic downfall of the Speaker on this occasion. He is the victim. He is a casualty of the government's overbearing conduct during this debate. We had done what we could do to prevent the government proceeding on the arrogant course which has produced this sorrowful result. That was our only recourse; that in fact was our only right. It was the duty of the Speaker to protect our rights just as it was his duty to protect the rights of the government.
Whatever may be said of the ugly things that happened here last week, I think it can be said with certainty that every hon. member is equally sorry that they ever happened. No hon. member of this house will want to see a repetition of the turmoil into which this house was thrown last Friday. Let it be admitted immediately that we all share some responsibility for that turmoil. We all took part in it. We can have no happy recollection at any time of that sad event. May I point out, however, that, confronted as we were with a rigid denial by the Speaker of our fundamental rights to be heard in regard to these issues, we had no course open to us but to register our anger in the way we did.

maintopic: MR. DREW    MOTION OF NON-CONFIDENCE IN PRESIDING OFFICER OF THE HOUSE
speechtext: Oh, oh! Hear, hear.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
maintopic: MR. DREW    MOTION OF NON-CONFIDENCE IN PRESIDING OFFICER OF THE HOUSE
speechtext:
Were we quietly to submit in the face of this course that savoured in every way of the dreadful dictatorships that have grown up in Europe in these past few years? It was Junius who said that the subject who is truly loyal will neither advise nor submit to arbitrary measures. The subject who is loyal will neither submit nor advise. We were not prepared to submit to as arbitrary measures as ever denied to the sitting members of a legislative body the rights to which they were entitled by tradition, by the rules and by all the declared purposes of this parliament. Mr. Speaker, this subject now is before the house. It is before the people of Canada. But, above all, it is now for the government to consider the course that it has followed and what it should do to deal with so grave a situation, with a situation which threatens the future of this house and of the rights of the people themselves as represented by the members here.
Under our system of government the Prime Minister (Mr. St. Laurent) must assume the first responsibility for all that happens under the government he leads. The fact that the course which led step by step to this inevitable result was initiated by the Minister of Trade and Commerce (Mr. Howe) in no way limits the responsibilities of the Prime Minister as head of the government. For all that happened here last Friday the Prime Minister must accept the responsibility. Most of us have little but sorrow in our hearts for the plight of the Speaker who was the victim of the government's action.
The Prime Minister could have prevented the dreadful scenes we witnessed here if he had asserted his authority along the lines of our parliamentary traditions. The Prime Minister saw where all this was heading. Starting with the motion of closure presented when the resolution was introduced that it was expedient for the pipe-line bill to come forward and following through step by step when the other arbitrary motions were presented, the Prime Minister saw what was happening in the house and he should have foreseen, as could be foreseen, what the consequences of that erosion must certainly be. I am not seeking for a moment to leave the impression that the opposition did not contribute to the disturbance, as did all the members on the other side. I repeat again, however, that we used the only weapons that we had as free men and women to bring to the attention of this house and to
House of Commons
the attention of the people of Canada the disgraceful denial of our rights which had taken place.
We had no choice but to assert our rights as we did. We had no choice, moreover, but to bring this matter to a head by the motion that is now before us. It is not necessary to enlarge upon the facts. Many incidents could be cited where step by step during these recent weeks we have gone along the course which has led to such a serious result. One truth does emerge, however. Beep are the wounds that have been inflicted upon parliament, and nothing that the Speaker can now do, nothing that the government can do, can restore this parliament to the atmosphere, to the state of mind, to the manners and to the decencies which existed here before these dreadful events occurred. I should like to quote words written by the great Gladstone in 1878 and published in the North American Review in the issue for September and October of that year. He said:
It is a cardinal axiom of the modern British constitution that the House of Commons is the greatest of the powers of the state. It might, by a base subserviency, fling itself at the feet of a monarch or a minister. . . . The commons are armed with ample powers of self-defence. If they use their powers properly, they can only be mastered by a recurrence to the people, and the way in which the appeal takes effect is by the choice of another House of Commons more agreeable to the national temper. Thus the sole appeal from the verdict of the house is a rightful appeal to those from whom it received its commission.
Here we had no power of self-defence. We have none but to declare what we believe to be the rights of the people of Canada and their representatives here in this house. We shall not be subservient to false interpretation of the rules. We shall not be subservient to anything that savours of dictatorship here in this house. We shall not be subservient to the will of the majority expressed by the Speaker, as it has been in this case, in a manner which no longer seeks to define the right of the majority but establishes for the time being mob rule.
I said before that I can only express sorrow for the plight of the Speaker on this occasion. The Prime Minister has the responsibility. He could have prevented this happening. He can prevent anything of a similar nature happening in the future. A partisan vote on the motion now before us will not relieve the unhappy situation in which we now find ourselves. Never before has this house been faced with so serious a situation. Never before were members of this house conscious as they now are that something good, decent, precious and valuable has been destroyed. There is only one way this situation can be relieved. I appeal with all

House of Commons
the earnestness I possess to the Prime Minister as head of the government to follow the only course which will restore the dignity, honour and traditions of parliament. That course is to dissolve this house and let the people elect a new parliament more in harmony with our traditions and concepts of government. To let this motion go to a vote that divides the house denies the very basis upon which the Speaker occupies the chair.
It has long been our tradition that the Speaker is the unanimous choice of the house. Let there be no uncertainty about the fact that the Speaker is not the choice of most of the members on this side of the house at this time. The situation can only be cured by the course that has been suggested. It can only be cured in the manner that was so well set out by Gladstone as long ago as 1878. That I believe is now the compelling duty confronting the Prime Minister of Canada (Mr. St. Laurent).
I support the motion that is now before the house.

maintopic: MR. DREW    MOTION OF NON-CONFIDENCE IN PRESIDING OFFICER OF THE HOUSE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I think all of us today assembled in this chamber realize the serious situation with which this house and the members of this house are confronted. I join with the Leader of the Opposition (Mr. Drew) in saying that, in my opinion, the introduction of this motion is something of a tragedy. I remember very well what took place about a year ago when a group of members of parliament in my office were discussing parliament and what had transpired. Among other things, we came to the conclusion that the time had arrived when this house might choose a Speaker who would preside over the house not for one parliament but for a number of years; and each and every one of us-may I say we were not of the language of the present Speaker of the house-were of the opinion that the present occupant of the chair at the end of this parliament should be offered that position on a longterm basis. I therefore say that what has happened at this session-and particularly what happened during the present debate-is indeed a tragic circumstance.
Quite early in the debate, Mr. Speaker-as no doubt you knew from a casual remark I made in the house-I thought that some of your rulings were partisan, and I so expressed myself to some of my friends on both sides of the house. As the days went by I felt that instead of there being protection of the rights of the minority, the majority opinion-that is government opinion-must of necessity prevail. I was saddened by that thought but then, as the time passed and various other rulings occurred and members who rose on this side of the house were denied the right,

now and then, which I thought was legitimately theirs to express their opinions on points of orders, that feeling turned more or less to anger.
I join with the Leader of the Opposition in saying that I am sure all of us regret the scene in this house last Friday afternoon. The bells were ringing even after some of us had risen to try to get a word in on a point of privilege which we felt was justifiable at the time. Members were called in to vote, I thought, without being given the opportunity to express themselves on a point of order or a question of privilege that I believe was really valid. I felt that the division had been hurried along in order, once again, to prevent those expressions of opinion that should have been heard by the Chair.
The Leader of the Opposition has, I think, fairly well expressed the view of those of us who felt that way. I think he has dealt with this problem. I have often disagreed with the Leader of the Opposition and probably on occasions shall do so again; but this afternoon I thought that the manner in which he dealt with this situation was a credit to him. He dealt with it in a statesmanlike and dignified manner and I hope that the example he set will be followed by all of us. He dealt with the events of Thursday evening and of Friday. I want to say just a word about that matter because I think that was the crucial point at which the opposition was really aroused. On Friday morning, as reported at page 4540 of Hansard, the Speaker said this:
. . . yesterday around 5.15, when I was called back to the chair for the purpose of receiving the chairman's report. I made a very serious mistake in allowing the point of order and the other dilatory motions; . . .
He then goes on to speak of the rights of the majority, with which I have no quarrel as long as the rights of the minority are safeguarded. Then he went on to say this:
I intend at the moment to submit to the house that, in my view, the house should revert to the position where it was yesterday when I was brought back to the chair to receive the chairman's report at 5.15. I submit to the house that the intervening proceedings should not be superseded, and it is up to the house to decide as to the situation which I take at the moment.
As has already been said, Mr. Speaker, this was a most unprecedented request to the house. Indeed it so surprised me that, as reported on the same page, I called out as loudly as I could, "What are you doing, Mr. Speaker?" I did so because I felt that what was being done was something that was going to stifle parliament in the future, change our procedure in the future, and make it possible on some other occasion for a Speaker to rise in his place and say that

the business which had been done heretofore should be wiped out. I thought that was a most unheard-of procedure.
Then later on the Speaker spoke of placing a proposition before the house. There was, of course, one way in which the Speaker could have got his views before the house, and that way has already been indicated. He could have got some member of the house to move an appropriate motion or to give notice of an appropriate motion. That was the proper procedure to follow if it was desired to make a change in what had already been done.
I am not going to speak very long because, as I have indicated, I do not think that any of us like the position in which we find ourselves. We do not like the breaches in those personal friendships that have been established over the years in this house. Some of us do not like the feeling that we have perhaps lost respect for one another. In this connection I should like to feel that we could go back to the position in which we found ourselves three weeks ago and wipe the slate clean. But that cannot be done. We must face up to this situation. There is no doubt, Mr. Speaker,-as the Leader of the Opposition has said-that no matter what we may do or say for the balance of this parliament, the Speaker has not the confidence of the entire house, something which is so necessary to conducting the business of this house. I agree with the Leader of the Opposition that, under these circumstances, there is only one way out. Regardless of our individual fortunes in an election period or of our party fortunes, I think that way out should be undertaken. It is the only way. I think that way should be taken in order that a new House of Commons might assemble in a few months' time; in order that that new House of Commons could come here with a new and fresh feeling; and in order that we might once more in this house establish the kind of atmosphere which has prevailed during most of the 21 years that I have been in this House of Commons.
I may say, Mr. Speaker, that this perhaps is unprecedented in our parliament. Of course, Mr. Gladstone refers to some of the turmoil in the British House of Commons, where events similar to those of last Friday have not been unknown even in the past half century and less. But it is today a great misfortune that we have to face the situation with which we are confronted. As the Leader of the Opposition (Mr. Drew) has said, and let none of us deny it, some responsibility rests on all of us.
The other afternoon I rose to speak and the shouting and so on from those on the 67509-295
House of Commons
other side was certainly enough to make one feel rather angry. I wish that I had suggested what I think might have been a way out at that time. In view of the tempers of hon. members of the house, the sittings might have been suspended while we cooled off a bit. But that was not done. So, we support the motion of the Leader of the Opposition. I suppose that it will be a vote directly along party lines. That seems to be indicated, and that is unfortunate. I know the feeling of my own friends. The Leader of the Opposition has indicated the feeling of his friends, and there is no doubt that there is no way out other than for the Prime Minister (Mr. St. Laurent) to dissolve this house and go to the country so that a new parliament, with all this sort of thing wiped out, may be assembled within the next few months.

I have listened with attention to the two previous speakers, and I agree with the leader of the C.C.F. party that the present situation is an unfortunate one. Let me say right at the start that I do not like the motion that is before the house. The suggestion that the government should resign as a solution is, of course, a suggestion that the government should surrender to the minority.
I listened to the Leader of the Opposition (Mr. Drew) and it seemed to me that his main weapon was that of exaggeration. It is true that he was able to keep himself fairly well controlled, mainly no doubt because there were no interruptions. He referred at length to what transpired in this house on May 31 and June 1. I would say that what transpired on Thursday and Friday cannot be judged by those days alone. It was the culmination of days of lawlessness in this house; shouting and defiance of the Speaker. I am not surprised that the Leader of the Opposition would say he would like to forget those days. It is not easy to forget what transpired in this house during that time. There was the phony display put on by the hon. member for Eglinton (Mr. Fleming) and action taken to deliberately force this house to expel him. We will not forget that. Hon. members can groan, but they should have been groaning at that time and not now.

speechtext:
The hon. member for Acadia (Mr. Quelch), Mr. Speaker, has just made two remarks which are a grave offence against privilege and a falsification of fact. He has referred to a "phony display" and has also

House of Commons
said that there was, on the part of the hon. member for Eglinton, an attempt to bring about a certain course of action that the house took. Mr. Speaker, there is not a measure of truth in one word, one syllable, one letter of what the hon. member said or what was said in my absence on Friday night by the hon. member for Iles-de-la-Madeleine (Mr. Cannon).
You know, and most members of this house know deep down in their hearts, that no member of this house was more surprised than I that the government took the partisan and vindictive course it did. The hon. member for Iles-de-la-Madeleine said, speaking on Friday night, that I had defied the Speaker. There was no defiance of the Speaker. He said also that the action on my suspension was the action of the chairman. It was nothing of the kind. My suspension was due to one thing and one thing alone, a government motion introduced by the Minister of Finance (Mr. Harris), the government leader. The first vote cast to suspend the hon. member for Eglinton was cast by the Prime Minister (Mr. St. Laurent). There was nothing premeditated. No one was more surprised than I.
The immediate situation that brought this about, as hon. members will remember, was one in which the Deputy Speaker of this house had said, while he was standing on his feet, he would not hear me on either a point of order or a question of privilege. He did hear the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre (Mr. Knowles) and he did say, at the very same time and under exactly the same circumstances, that he would hear my colleague the hon. member for Greenwood (Mr. Macdonnell), but he would not hear me. That was the situation, and that was the fact. Any member, whether in this house or outside, who says I sought to provoke this suspension, had any idea that it would be made or made a show here for the purposes of publicity commits the most vile kind of falsehood. Let there be no mistake about that.
I just make one further observation. It has been said outside the house by the hon. member for Timiskaming (Mrs. Shipley) that there was something very strange about the appearance of the flag. I want to say this. When I took my departure from the house that day following the passing of this partisan and vindictive motion, I did not know there was any flag going to be put on my desk.

Mr. Speaker, so far as the point the hon. member has raised is concerned, I will just say this. I will allow those hon. members who sat in this house at that time to decide whether or not the statement I made was correct. We had the display put on from time to time by the hon. member for Kamloops (Mr. Fulton). I could not help thinking at the time that probably the hon. member had taken so much time in reading crime comics he had absorbed the mentality of a juvenile delinquent.
The Speaker of this house is the unfortunate victim of circumstances that were not of his making. I think that this is something we must keep in mind at all times. He was not responsible for the situation that developed in this house during the past few days. I think most of us will agree, and the Leader of the Opposition has already stated it, that he had earned a fine reputation for impartiality and for fairness. I would say that he invariably leaned over backwards in order to meet the requests of the opposition, and it was probably that very action that got him into trouble in this debate. It is a very fine way to act in normal times but you cannot act that way in times of lawlessness because those who are committing those acts will take advantage of that type of leniency.
Let me go back to May 9 when this matter first came up. The opposition has blamed closure for their obstruction but of course that is not true. It started several days before the motion for closure was moved; that is, when the notice of motion first appeared in Votes and Proceedings on May 9 it started and it continued on May 10, a long procedural wrangle with four divisions, and then resumed again on May 14 when two more divisions and more wrangling took place. Finally, when the Minister of Trade and Commerce spoke, he moved closure, no doubt because the government realized that so long as the opposition was going to

continue that type of wrangling and obstruction there would have been no hope of ever getting that bill through without closure.
Again I stress the fact obstruction started first and closure followed. The opposition then became angry as a result of closure being moved, but unfortunately instead of fighting the government or the measure they should have fought they vented their spleen and their spite upon the Speaker, the Deputy Speaker and the chairman, and in my opinion that was a cowardly procedure to follow.
Since then they have tried to dictate to parliament. They have tried as a minority to tell the majority how the affairs of this house should be conducted. We have seen in other countries what happened when a minority is allowed to dictate to the majority. We saw that when Hitler was borne to power, then Mussolini was borne to power, and we have seen it in Russia, and we do not want that kind of thing to happen in this country. You cannot appease that type of mentality. Every time you appease that type of mentality they want more concessions.
Instead of debating the legislation before us the opposition staged a number of attacks against the Speaker, the Deputy Speaker and the chairman. It has been said by those on my right that we in the Social Credit group have nothing to talk about in relation to this matter because we filibustered the Bretton Woods agreement and on the rivers bill; but let me point out that there is a great difference between the filibuster we staged and the one we have witnessed in this house during the past two or three weeks. When we opposed the Bretton Woods agreement and the rivers bill we attacked the legislation. We did not at any time enter into a procedural wrangle and we never defied the chairman or the Speaker.

This has not failed to be obvious to persons outside the house. I have here a clipping from the Montreal Star-not an unimportant newspaper in this country. It is from its edition of May 30 and is headed "The Speaker's Dilemma". It reads in part as follows:
The Speaker's first duty is to keep the business of the House of Commons moving smoothly. When the opposition embarks upon a planned campaign of obstruction, it is obvious that the Speaker (or, in committee of the whole, the chairman) will become a target of attack-
Not because of the qualities of the Speaker or the chairman but because of the fact that there is a contentious measure that is being opposed by all means that can be devised under the rules of the house to bring about delay and to waste time.
' The editorial continues:
Every restriction on debate, from the sharp weapon of closure down to the hour-by-hour * rulings of its presiding officers, is challenged in extreme terms-so extreme indeed that they arouse laughter and contempt among the thinking public which is not so dumb as to believe that free discussion is being slaughtered.
I think the concluding paragraph should .-also be put on the record. It reads:
As to Mr. Beaudoin's present unhappy position, a study of recent Hansards reveals an extraordinary patience and courtesy in dealing with a series of heated situations. He has proved himself to be a good Speaker. When the present row is over, and tempers have cooled off, it would not be surprising to hear compliments about his conduct from the opposition benches.
What is it that has brought about the unfortunate situation in which we find ourselves at this moment? On Thursday I made *a motion to apply closure based upon a 1932 precedent. A point of order was raised by the hon. member for Kamloops (Mr. Fulton). That was one point of order in this whole long series to which I took no exception whatsoever. I did think that when the .government was resorting to a procedure so rarely used as standing order 33 has been, and when there were two precedents which might be applied, it was a quite proper question to raise as to which was the really valid precedent. I am sure that all hon. members on both sides of the house will admit that we on this side listened with great respect to the arguments presented from the other side of the house. I attempted to present an argument in support of the precedent we were invoking. In due course, and not until every hon. member who desired to speak on the point of order had had an opportunity to be heard, did the chairman make his ruling. That ruling was immediately appealed 'toy the hon. member for Winnipeg North

Centre (Mr. Knowles) and the appeal was reported to Your Honour.
It was at this point, if, with respect, I may use the words you used, that a mistake was made-you used those words the following morning-but nowhere in the use or application of those words was there any suggestion to declare as a nullity what had taken place from the time you referred to as being the moment when you made the mistake of not enforcing the usual practice that you were back in the chair merely for the purpose of receiving a report from the chairman of the committee, and putting the appeal which had been made on the question contained in the report to the house for its decision. You did commence to put that question. You had previously ruled on numerous occasions that when such an appeal came before you through the report of a chairman there was nothing else before the house and that that report had to be put to a vote.
The hon. member for Winnipeg South Centre (Mr. Churchill) rose and raised a point upon what appeared to me and what appeared to many to be an academic question. You allowed him to proceed and he did proceed at considerable length. After he had submitted his point and when you were on the point of making your ruling, it was suggested to you that you should not complete your ruling until after six o'clock. We all know what took place after the dinner recess. We know that there were then various proceedings which were obviously undertaken for the purpose of taking up time and preventing the report from the chairman of the committee being submitted to the house and the house getting back into committee.
In the course of the discussion Your Honour indicated to the house that the point raised by the hon. member for Winnipeg South Centre was merely an academic point and there was nothing on which to rule. Your Honour then proceeded to put the question on the appeal of the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre, the question which was before the house, the only question which could be before the house at that particular time. Your Honour had actually called the yeas and, according to Hansard, you were about to call the nays when the hon. member for Winnipeg South Centre, although Your Honour was on your feet, rose in an insistent manner and demanded an appeal from a ruling Your Honour had not made. The appeal was granted and Your Honour's opinion was sustained on the appeal.
At this point the hon. member for Quebec West (Mr. Dufresne), although a motion to adjourn the house had previously been disposed of and had taken, as these proceedings do take in our house, about three-quarters of

an hour, renewed a motion for the adjournment of the house. That motion was put and decided and according to page 4528 of Hansard Your Honour then rose and said the following words:
The question is now, shall we-
At that point the hon. member for Nanaimo (Mr. Cameron) rose and raised what you have since declared to be an improper question of privilege and which I am informed the hon. gentleman himself was astonished to find was taken seriously. On this the hon. member founded a motion which Your Honour put to the house. At that point the Leader of the Opposition (Mr. Drew) rose to speak and after he had proceeded briefly he asked this question:
Do I gather that some members opposite do not think the rules were properly applied?
That was the first opportunity that any member of the government had had to raise a point of order. The Minister of Finance (Mr. Harris) raised again the point of order which he had raised at six o'clock and once more drew Your Honour's attention to the fact that no intervening business could occur, and that the only purpose of Your Honour being in the chair was to put the appeal of the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre which had been reported to the house at 5.15. The remarks made at that moment by the Minister of Finance will be found at page 4531. When the hon. Leader of the Opposition said this afternoon that there had been no objection to the course which was being followed he evidently overlooked this paragraph in the second column of page 4531, which reads:

Normally when a member brings to the attention of the house an article which concerns privilege and in which someone in the house is involved, after he has made his motion it is up to the other member
House of Commons
involved to be heard. If hon. members care to debate this matter before I myself am heard on the subject, I am not going to object; I am just going to let them go right ahead, but at one stage of the proceedings I want to say that I will have to be heard.
There was no decision made upon the point of order or the motion. The motion was before you, and on that and on another occasion you had suggested that the matter should not be further considered but should be adjourned. As recorded at the foot of the second column of page 4532, this is what you said, sir:
As regards the article by Mr. Eugene Forsey, in which he writes under the title "About Closure, the Speaker, and Rights of Parliament", there may be more paragraphs there which are incriminatory, but certainly not the whole of the article. I repeat the suggestion I made earlier, that this matter for the moment be adjourned.
Your suggestion was not accepted, and the Leader of the Opposition said:
Mr. Speaker, with deference, I do not believe this should be adjourned.
He went on to discuss the matter until we reached the hour of ten o'clock. You had already made it quite clear that you felt you might have to make a ruling upon the question at some time. You stated at that time that you were sufficiently informed and did not need to hear any further discussion on the point of order, or the matter as to whether or not this was a proper motion relating to privilege.
Sir, it has always been my understanding that points of order were not matters for debate. Points of order were matters to be decided by the Speaker, about which any remarks that were made by hon. members were not remarks in the form of a debate but remarks designed to inform the Speaker, to call his attention to certain other precedents or to what should, in their view, be the manner in which the point of order should be decided.
These rules in their application, sir, are made to protect the rights of parliament in the psychological atmosphere where the business of parliament is being carried out. They are not rules designed to furnish weapons to delay the passage of the regular business of the house. If it were to be decided that when a point of order is raised it is a subject that is open to debate for every hon.

The editorial reads:
The pipe line debate in the House of Commons began formally on May 10, though the subject had been frequently discussed long before that date. Today is June 2, ample time, one would think, for adequate public discussion of the merits and demerits of the legislation. The bill, however, has not yet passed. The government, on the other hand, is equally determined to pass the pipe line bill into law, as it possesses a large majority in the House of Commons, its success is likely.

To the prejudice of the government's position. With respect to the procedure in the house the Minister of Finance, as leader of the house, had drawn Your Honour's attention to this disregard of the rules and practice, first in the 67509-296
House of Commons
afternoon and then in the evening of Thursday. On neither occasion had Your Honour seen fit to rule on the point of order raised by the Minister of Finance. When on Friday Your Honour put to the house the question that the house, which is the master of its own proceedings, should be placed in exactly the same position it was when you resumed the chair on Thursday to submit the chairman's ruling, you were met by very strong objections and there occurred the incidents which we all deplore.
Now I recognize, sir, that strong feelings and great heat have been demonstrated in this debate. I recognize that hon. gentlemen opposite felt, and probably still feel, that the government has applied standing order 33 with undue severity. We do not feel we have done so. We have acted within the rules to protect the rights of all hon. members on both sides of the house to express their opinion by their vote on this measure in time to be effective. There is a legitimate difference between two sides of the house; it is the normal working of our parliamentary system. On Thursday, I will not deny we were disappointed at the manner in which the rules had been applied, but we created no scene. We made no manifestation. We submitted to that.
On Friday Your Honour, having examined the situation and having come to the conclusion that you should at the first opportunity put the appeal that normally should have been put at five o'clock on the day before, without nullifying any proceeding, you proceeded to submit to the house the question as to whether that should be done. The house having approved that course, you did so.
There was, and still is apparently, the suggestion that in doing so you were subordinating the rules of parliament to the will of the government. Well, we absolutely repudiate any such suggestion. We do say that proceedings of the character of this motion would constitute a very serious precedent that would enable any factious group that was opposed to any bit of legislation to resort to it, and thus prevent the normal operations of the House of Commons in the progress of its business. I should like at this point to refer very briefly to something that was said by an hon. member who was the then hon member for Vancouver East, as recorded at page 41 of Hansard for January 28, 1949:
Surely this is a question of orderly procedure in parliament, and whether we agree with it or not is a matter to be decided by the vote of parliament.
It has been stated, and we must all recognize it, that if there are hon. members who are prepared to vote for this motion

House of Commons
there are very many more on both sides of the house who are prepared to assert by their votes that they still have confidence in the presiding officer of this house. Such a vote would not be a happy situation. It may be an inevitable situation. It is one about which those who have spoken for the other three groups in the house have made their positions clear.
I feel that, on this side of the house, we are entitled to some time for the consideration of what should be the ultimate disposition of this motion. It is not a situation which cannot be cured. It is not a situation which is going to destroy this parliament; and there should be in the minds of reasonable men, after they have had an opportunity of expressing their views, the feeling that, after all, something has to be done to allow parliament to continue to operate in the true traditions of British institutions and to carry on its work effectively. This would not be achieved by the adaption of this kind of motion, and is not apt to be achieved by the repudiation of this kind of motion, no matter what the majority opposed to it.
I therefore move at this time, seconded by the Minister of Finance (Mr. Harris):

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the manner in which the Prime Minister (Mr. St. Laurent) has introduced this motion for third reading is as accurate an expression of the attitude of the government toward the business of the house and towards the house itself as anything which has come before the house in recent days. It displays the utter contempt of the government for parliament and for the business that is before the house. The Prime Minister as head of the government on this occasion chose to rise on the third reading of a bill which relates to what has been described to us as one of the greatest and most important ventures to come before this country for some considerable time, and simply tell us that there is not very much that requires to be said.
There is a great deal that requires to be said. There is a great deal that requires to be said about the steps by which we have come to this ignominous position in dealing with this bill. We have had exactly the same conduct on the part of the government at each stage, but at least it can be said that on no earlier occasion was there such a summary dismissal of the proceedings before parliament as that *with which the Prime Minister has placed (before the house for third reading a bill of .such importance as is suggested by government spokesmen.
Then again, there was the statement by the Prime Minister, in the very few words he spoke before he again applied the gag, that there had been no suggestion that there should be any change in the language or form of this legislation. What a travesty on what has taken place. There were plenty of changes that were going to be made. There were (plenty of changes that would have been suggested if the government had dealt in an orderly and sensible way with the legislation which is now before the house.
Let us just review what has taken place, now that we have reached the very final stage, again under the shadow of the axe. The first stage in the introduction of the bill was a motion standing in the name of the Minister of Trade and Commerce (Mr. Howe) that it was expedient that the bill be introduced. That was the first step. That motion was brought before the house long months after it had been announced in the speech from the throne that legislation of this nature would be brought before us. The government waited until the very last possible day to introduce this legislation, and then has talked of the need of haste.
In January the government knew what was needed. In January the government, in the speech from the throne, stated that we would
,[Mr. Diefenbaker.l

receive legislation of this kind; yet it only came before us three weeks ago today. That is the haste that has been precipitated and forced on this house by the government as a result of its dilatory conduct since this legislation was first announced on January 10 of this year.
When the resolution came forward three weeks ago today, before a single word had been said by any member of the opposition the Minister of Trade and Commerce introduced the first closure motion. That was unprecedented in the history of this house. That was the use of the axe in the most coldblooded manner. Never before has anyone ever thought of introducing closure before there has even been an indication from the opposition as to its views on the particular measure in question. Do not let anyone say there had been views expressed before. This measure only came forward in these very recent weeks after the government had decided to change its original course and halt the proceedings which began on March 15 of this year.
Then in the ordinary course of events we came to second reading. Again there was closure. Then we came to the committee stage, which is the stage where the bill can be discussed in detail. The Prime Minister says today there was no suggestion that there should be any changes in the language or form. What chance did the government give us to deal with this bill properly? None whatever. The moment clause 1 was called the Minister of Trade and Commerce immediately applied a particularly vicious form of closure and moved the adjournment of consideration of that clause. The moment clause 2 was called the same procedure was followed. Again there was closure of this special type. Clause 2 is the defining clause, the clause that tells us what the terms mean, all the terms that give meaning to the language and form-to use the words of the Prime Minister-of the rest of the act.
Then the third clause was the clause which established a corporation. The Prime Minister said, "Oh, we thought we would just pass over these clauses so we could come to the clauses that were the important ones". That clause establishing the corporation was an important clause, as also was clause 2. Then clause 4 was called. Obviously at that time the ears of the government had been opened a little, not too much, and it was decided to permit a limited amount of debate. On that occasion there was actually a discussion on clause 4.
Mr. Speaker, there has been talk of obstruction. The delay there has been, the discussion there has been, has related to the

rights of the members of this house as representatives of the people of Canada, and the discussion which has taken place here has been a fight for the right of the people of Canada to have their legislation properly presented in this house.
Now the legislation is before us in its final stage, and it is clear that the government is not prepared to concede the possibility of any change. In what it has done today in moving closure once again the government makes it clear that it is determined to go ahead with this act unrevised and unchanged.
This act is a mongrel if ever there was one. We have first of all an act that was framed with the idea of setting up the Northern Ontario Pipe Line Crown Corporation. Then instead of revising the act to make it an intelligible piece of legislation we find that the government has left there part II which has nothing to do with the northern Ontario part of the line but which provides for the section of 574 miles from the Alberta boundary to the vicinity of Winnipeg.
This act in its dual form does two strange things. First of all it sets up a crown corporation which is going to receive-if the act is passed as the government is determined it shall be-$130 million of public funds. For what purpose is that $130 million advanced? For the purpose of building the northern Ontario section of the pipe line. Is that $130 million to be used for that purpose? Certainly not within the framework of this act for the time being, because part II of the act provides that of that $130 million up to $80 million is to be advanced, by the crown corporation set up for the purpose of building the northern Ontario pipe line, to Trans-Canada Pipe Lines for the purpose of building that western section. That is not one of the declared purposes of the Northern Ontario Pipe Line Crown Corporation, and it is not a proper use of the funds that are to be advanced to the Northern Ontario Pipe Line Crown Corporation.
We objected in the first instance to the advancing of Canadian funds in this way to build a pipe line, to the use of Canadian money for the purpose of handing over a pipe line to a company which is 83 per cent United States owned. Again we have this confused picture; Canadian money is to be used for the purpose of financing a venture that was to have been financed by the Trans-Canada Pipe Lines company itself. But we have this dual arrangement: Advance the money for the construction of the western portion and deny immediately to the Northern Ontario Pipe Line Crown Corporation the opportunity to build, until that money is repaid, the part of the pipe line which it was intended to
4, 1956	4665
Northern Ontario Pipe Line Corporation build. That is using this crown corporation's money for a purpose that was never intended.
Mr. Speaker, over and over again we have heard talk about the desire of this government to welcome investment from the United States. It is not getting the investment from the United States. We have heard from this government that Canadians cannot finance this effort. Canadians are going to finance this effort simply because this government is going to use the Canadian taxpayers' money, whether or not they want it to do so. They are not even going to let the Canadian taxpayer have a chance to say what he wants done about this matter. We have urged for some time that this government take this matter to the people. There was never any suggestion that the Canadian taxpayers' money was to be used for the financing of a venture of this kind. The government has no mandate whatever to use the Canadian taxpayers' money in this way.
Whether or not the money will be repaid by Trans-Canada Pipe Lines, the fact remains that to the extent of over $200 million this government is proceeding to help to finance this United States-controlled organization. Let it not be said that this is just an advance which will be repaid. From time to time we hear of rotating funds. This is a rotating fund if, in fact, it rotates. This is a fund which, first of all, helps in the financing of the western section up to 90 per cent of the cost, and then in one way or another proceeds with the construction of the northern Ontario section if the government goes ahead with that venture.
Whether Trans-Canada Pipe Lines repays or not, the financing of the western section up to $80 million is to be done with public money; and then in turn, if the government proceeds, up to $130 million is to be used by the crown corporation for the construction of the northern Ontario section. That means- and it means nothing else-that over $200 million of public money is to be used in helping to finance a company which said it could finance this whole venture without government assistance.
Here we are at the third reading stage and the Prime Minister, instead of telling us today that there was not very much to be said, could well have been explaining to us at this late date why it is that he is now supporting a plan which he said last year he did not like. He has not yet at any stage explained when the transition occurred and when he moved from plan 1 and plan 2 to plan 3 and gave it his blessing and approval. Not only has he not explained why he is accepting this plan which he did not like, namely the northern Ontario construction under the

Northern Ontario Pipe Line Corporation crown corporation. He certainly has not explained in any satisfactory way how he justifies that still greater expenditure of public money to build this western section in the way it is to be built.
Last night I listened to a panel discussion over television, when a number of men who have interested themselves in the trans-Canada pipe line were discussing this subject. One of the things which interested me greatly was the extent to which even those who have followed this matter very closely do not yet realize that there has been a great departure from the original plan and that, far from having a venture which is being financed by United States investment, we now have the reverse of what was originally proposed here in this House of Commons; that instead of having a venture financed by United States investment, we have a venture financed by Canadian taxpayers' money and the advantages turned over to a company that is controlled in the United States, under an arrangement which will give the profits to the stockholders in the United States.
I have said this before and now on this motion for third reading I say it once again: If a group of Canadian investors, headed by someone who happened to know the minister responsible at Washington, went down there and asked them to put up the funds of the United States taxpayers to finance a Canadian venture which would have substantial control over great gas resources in the United States, does any hon. member opposite suggest for a moment that there would be the slightest chance of any person in congress doing anything but laughing at the proposal?

These are the figures in the order in which they appear as the average rate per thousand cubic feet: Saskatchewan, 26-6 cents; Manitoba, Winnipeg and Central Gas, 32-9 cents; others, 35 cents; Midwestern Gas Transmission at Emerson, 25-3 cents. That is the place where the gas is sold to the United States. Ontario Union Gas Company, 39 cents; western Ontario to other distributors, 42-2 cents; northern Ontario, 52 * 7 cents; International Nickel, 51-5 cents; North Bay to Toronto, 77-5 cents; Provincial Gas Company, 46-1 cents; Dominion Gas Company, 66 [DOT] 2 cents; Toronto and area, 51-5 cents; east of Toronto to Montreal, 54-7 cents; Ottawa and area, 52-1 cents; undistributed gas delivered at Niagara, 35 [DOT] 67 cents; Quebec-Montreal, 52-1 cents.
