Neither the Prime Minister nor any hon. member opposite who adheres to the truth can suggest that they were not given ample opportunity at each stage to provide all the information that was required. In the speech from the throne read on January 10 it was stated that legislation to incorporate a crown corporation would be brought forward. In January I asked that this be referred to a committee so that information could be obtained. I have continued right through this session to ask that this be referred to a committee so we could obtain the information which was essential.
We came into the various stages where there has been closure, and now there is closure on third reading to be applicable tomorrow. We have wanted information, we have sought information. We would like information from Trans-Canada Pipe Lines as to why these deals were made to the disadvantage of Canadian purchasers. Those are the kind of things we want.
Then in case once again the Prime Minister should suggest that we have delayed proceedings here let me remind you that we made a perfectly clear submission on March 15, now considerably more than two and a half months ago. When the first motion for the setting up of the crown corporation was presented to this house I had this to say, and I place it on the record again. I pointed out that there were certain suggestions which I wanted to place before the house. Let no one now suggest that we only came forward at the last minute to ask that this be referred to a committee or that other applicants have an opportunity to build this pipe line and to be heard. Over two and a half months ago this is what I said, as reported at page 2182 of Hansard of March 15:
Before I close I want to put certain suggestions before the house and for the consideration of the government, in the hope that they may be prepared to listen to the words of the Prime Minister when he told the house last year that he did not like this method. First, refer the whole question immediately to a committee of this house to obtain the facts and make appropriate recommendations. Second, insist upon the reorganization of Trans-Canada Pipe Lines as an all-Canadian company which can proceed immediately and under Canadian control. Third, if Trans-Canada cannot carry out its undertaking, then open the whole matter and permit new interests to make their proposals for an all-Canadian line, Canadian controlled. Fourth, if it can be shown, and I doubt that it is so, that part of the pipe line must be built as the government asserts on this occasion, then instead of building a part which could become an orphan under certain circumstances in the future, let them build the whole pipe line and lease it for operation under Canadian control.
rMr. Drew.]

That was the proposal which I placed before the government in explicit terms on March 15 of this year. If a committee had been set up at that time it could have heard all the evidence which would have been submitted. We could have heard from Mr. McMahon, and there is a lot more to be heard about that. The Minister of Finance may laugh but I think the minister knows a great deal more about the McMahon transaction than he has yet disclosed. I think there are other ministers whom I could name who know a great deal more about it and who are not as uninformed on this subject as was the Prime Minister. The Prime Minister had heard nothing whatever about Mr. McMahon's proposal until after the new agreement had been made with Trans-Canada following their default. I think perhaps the Minister of Finance had heard. I should like to hear from him what he knew about Mr. McMahon.
At any rate we have the right to know, and I suggested on March 15 that this should go to a committee so we could obtain information. If that committee had been set up we could have had Mr. Gairdner of Gairdner and Company come here so we could find out what their proposal was. In addition to that we could also have had Mr. Champion come here, whose information was placed before the Minister of Finance. There would also have been many other Canadians who would have come before that committee if it had been set up. What is certain is that there were a great many Canadians who could have undertaken this task if they had received as favourable terms as are being offered by this government to the United States-controlled company now before us, but this government refuses to consider the setting up of a committee.
Every relatively unimportant bill that comes to this house dealing with a matter connected with transportation is referred automatically, as a matter of course, to the committee on railways, canals and telegraph lines. Any small rail line, any small transportation operation that comes before this house by way of a measure to build it or to set it up or to give it rights is submitted automatically to that committee.
Why not in this case? The fact is that in those cases they have nothing to conceal. They expect to have to bring the facts out into the open. In this case the government was not ready to let us have that ordinary committee inquiry to which we were entitled as a matter of course. I need not point out, of course, that every one of these pipe-line applications in the first instance was submitted to that committee. Every charter,

when the application was made, was submitted to this committee automatically before it was dealt with. Why not in this case? I think the answer is clear, but do not let the Prime Minister suggest to us that we did not offer in plenty of time an opportunity for all the facts to be obtained.
Now we recognize the fact that if the Trans-Canada company were prepared to carry out its undertakings, then under the ordinary contractual obligations it would have the right to do so. I remind this house again that when we spoke about the reorganization of Trans-Canada Pipe Lines, we were suggesting that action in view of the fact that this was the organization which without any reservation had stated in this house through its spokesman that it could construct the whole Canadian line without any export and without government assistance. As a matter of fact as recently as last year Mr. Clint Murchison, the favoured figure for this whole transaction, the man who has the largest single block of shares in this whole transaction, this wealthy man who does not put out his money unless he has to-and he certainly is not being called upon to do so in this case-in his letter to the Minister of Trade and Commerce left no doubt about his assertion that this could be built without government assistance. Then all this has fallen apart.
How they must be laughing at us. How Mr. Clint Murchison and Mr. Gardiner Symonds and the other United States promoters associated with this operation must be laughing at us here. They get the charter on the promise that they can build the line and then, just because they are the only people that know everything about it, this government promises to do the major financing with the Canadian taxpayers' money. What nonsense to suggest that these are the only people who can do it. Look at a map of the gas transmission lines in the United States. They are like the veins in the human body. We could engage the services of experts from any one company or scores of companies that have had experience in this line. There is no question about the possibility of being able to get expert skill of this kind that is needed.
Then I go back to the fact that if Trans-Canada was not able to carry out its undertakings, then it had no right to be the chosen instrument any longer. Under those circumstances I proposed on behalf of our party that if Trans-Canada could not carry out this undertaking, then the whole matter should be placed before the committee and the opportunity presented for offers to be made. After all, it was well over two and a half

The moment this passes and they set up the corporation to build this northern segment, then they are setting up a corporation which will build 675 miles of this pipe line as a publicly-owned pipe line. That being the case, let us see the result.
We have this strange picture. We have the western section of 574 miles from the Alberta border to the vicinity of Winnipeg, to be financed by the Canadian taxpayers' money to the extent of $80 million, or up to 90 per cent of the cost of construction. Then there is the stretch of 110 miles between Winnipeg and the Ontario boundary. We do not know yet how the government is going to help finance that. We have not been told a word about that, not a word as to how they are going to link up the Winnipeg Section with the northern Ontario section. Then comes the northern Ontario section of 674 miles to be built by a crown corporation. Beyond that is the section of 432 miles from Kapuskasing

Northern Ontario Pipe Line Corporation to Toronto, and then the pipe line from Toronto to Montreal to complete the whole line.
How are these others to be built? We do not know that, but we know that this government is committing this parliament and the people of Canada to public construction of a stretch of 675 miles across northern Ontario. Now we are on third reading. We have passed the preliminary committee stage. We have passed the stage when this could be discussed on second reading and the principles considered. speechtext:
"Public ownership", I hear on the other side. Yes, this government is committing us to public ownership. This government is placing before us now a bill to set up a crown corporation to build 675 miles under public ownership, but then adds this mongrel arrangement under which it puts up the taxpayers' money to hand over to Trans-Canada Pipe Lines to build the other section out in the west, and does not even tell us what it is going to do with the 110 miles between Winnipeg and the Ontario boundary or the stretch between Kapuskasing and Toronto. This pipe line through northern Ontario, if they get to that stage, could be an orphan.
Now, Mr. Speaker, we believe that if a committee had been set up, if the proper inquiry had taken place, this whole line could have been built by Canadians under such a plan of private ownership as has been set forth in this house. However, we recognize now that this stage is past. We recognize now that this government commits itself here on third reading to proceeding with public ownership of a part of the line. It would be an absurd position to have public ownership of the 675 miles and then have private ownership of the parts on both sides,


with all the conflicting difficulties which: would be raised by that situation.
There would also be the fact that if for any reason Trans-Canada Pipe Lines did not fulfil its undertakings-and it will be the first time it did if it does now-then in that case the government would be left with an orphan. There would be only one thing the government could do and that would be to proceed to expropriate any other parts of the line then in existence to complete the whole line. Let us anticipate that, then. If we had had the opportunity in committee to deal with these matters we could have made recommendations.
The Prime Minister said today that we made no suggestions. We were not given the opportunity. There could have been proposals. Now, on third reading, we say to the government: You want to get ahead with the pipe line. All right, if you are determined to follow the course of going ahead with the-pipe line with a crown corporation, go ahead with it but expand the crown corporation and give that crown corporation the power to build the whole line from the Alberta boundary right through to the east. That was what I said on March 15, and I repeat it:
Therefore if it comes to the stage where this-government forces through an unnecessary venture of this kind, then there is only one thing to do and that is build the whole pipe line and not just part of it, and have control over the whole line.
Now, Mr. Speaker, the government surely is not going to tell us that it cannot obtain the pipe to proceed with this construction. That pipe has been ordered for this particular construction. There is no other operation on the North American continent that is at this moment in need of 34-inch pipe. If the crown corporation is expanded and given authority to build the whole line it can, without any question, acquire that 34-inch pipe to proceed with the western section right away, and there need be no delay.
But just at this point let me deal with the suggestion that has been made that there might be two or three years' delay if we do not proceed, no matter what the terms are, with this chosen instrument of the government, Trans-Canada Pipe Lines. Why, Mr. Speaker, this 34-inch pipe was only ordered last October, and it was proceeding to delivery in six months' time. There is no reason in the world why similar pipe cannot be obtained at any time within six months after the order has been placed. But that is only a speculative proposition. Talk of two and three years is sheer and unadulterated nonsense, the kind of bluffing this government has been doing from the very beginning in connection with this whole operation.

Let them go ahead. Let them introduce a bill to expand the operation of the crown corporation to embrace the whole line. They can get the pipe. They can proceed with the construction; we can assure control of the pipe line for Canadians, and we can assure prices that are advantageous to Canadians instead of permitting big gas operators in the United States to set prices that will be unduly favourable to them. In this way if the government, having committed itself to public construction under a crown corporation for the 675 miles, will expand that operation to embrace the whole line, it can start immediately. It can start with the pipe that is available and with the skill that is available as well.
In that way we will have Canadian gas moving in Canada and we will be able then to lead from strength and not from weakness. If we want to get the best prices for Canadian gas in the export market the surest way to get those prices is not to be dependent upon permission to enter the export market. The best way is for us to have our own line and then, having our own line, make the best deal we can and be sure that we are not simply being taken for a ride by the Tennessee Gas company and their subsidiaries in the United States. Now, Mr. Speaker, this is now in its final stage.

Northern Ontario Pipe Line Corporation delivered us, gagged and muzzled, into the hands of this powerful group of United States oil magnates.
That is what is happening in this country today, and when we are fighting this proposition we are fighting to preserve the right of this country to control its own destiny. We have watched our natural resources, resource after resource, slip into the hands of powerful foreign companies for processing, so that our iron ore goes from this country and steel comes back at a high price and high profit. Our pulp and paper crosses the line and comes back to us in the form of all sorts of magazines, some of which are good and some of which are objectionable. It also comes back in various other forms. Now we are going to give them one of the greatest sources of power, if this Tennessee Gas company can secure licences from the federal power commission to import the gas into the United States.
I welcomed tonight the statement of the Leader of the Opposition that the first three propositions he made some time ago are now beyond the realm of possibility and that consequently he falls back on the fourth proposition he made on March 15, that this line should be built by the public of Canada, owned by the public of Canada, controlled by the public of Canada and operated by the public of Canada to distribute across Canada first a valuable and great Canadian natural resource. That has been the position we have taken from the outset.
Oh yes; we have been told there are difficulties in the way of the government operating a line like this. Of course there are difficulties. The government would have to negotiate for the gas with the producers in Alberta. How many producers are there in Alberta? In the main not more than a dozen companies are involved, and those companies are United States companies who have gained control, and I am not blaming them. I am not blaming even the province of Alberta, in the financial situation in which the provinces find themselves, for entering into the agreements, although I cannot agree with some of the ideas behind the Alberta agreements with the companies which discovered oil and gas in that province. But I am saying it is not a case of negotiating with thousands of producers; it is a case of purchasing, if you will, gas from wells that are under the control of a few powerful private corporations.
I know that the president of Gulf Oil company stated some months ago that he would not allow his gas to be used by any corporation in which the government was involved. Who does he think he is? This

Northern Ontario Pipe Line Corporation United States financier comes into Canada and tells the Canadian people that he will not allow them to use one of their own great resources. Where has this country got to; where is this country going?
I want to say, as I have said before in connection with this matter, that if this kind of thing continues for any greater length of time the day will come when we shall have lost our economic independence and will be dependent upon the United States of America. An attempt will be made ultimately to make this country part of that one. I want none of that, because in spite of all the disappointments we have suffered in this parliament in recent days I still believe that the parliamentary system of government is better, provided we can preserve it, than any other form of government of which I know. But in the past two weeks we have seen it steadily undermined by a government which should be doing its best, particularly in these days, to preserve it and the autonomy of our country.
It is said it would be difficult for the federal government to distribute this gas to consumers. I grant that immediately. We have never suggested that the federal government should distribute the gas. What we have said is what Mr. Leslie Frost, the premier of Ontario, said some time ago. Remember that Mr. Frost only accepted this, as the Ontario Hansard bears out, because it was the federal government that had made the decision. When the bill was introduced into the Ontario legislature, Mr. Porter and Mr. Frost made it abundantly clear that their bill was drafted in such a manner that if this parliament felt the present proposition unwise or if for any reason the present plan fell through, they could enter into any other arrangement with the government of Canada. That was his original idea.
I want to say tonight that under a plan whereby the government would own and operate the main gas line the gas could be distributed by any means a province desired to use. If a province wished to distribute the gas by a private enterprise corporation the government could enter into an agreement with that private enterprise corporation to distribute it. But my expectation is that the provinces would do as they have done with electricity, that they would decide to distribute gas through public ownership.
Under this plan the figures produced by the Minister of Trade and Commerce and even tonight by the Leader of the Opposition may make some people think they are going to get pretty cheap gas. But when we look at the figures for the city of Winnipeg, for example, we get some idea of what they are

I do sincerely hope that what has been said by both hon. members who have spoken before me, and the recognition that it is likely this bill will receive third reading some time in the next few days, will remove a great many of the difficulties under which we have laboured.
Now, I heartily agree with all that has been said today. I sincerely hope we can get back to our old standard of conduct, and I will join with both members opposite in saying that I understand, under the circumstances, how strongly they may feel about the conditions attendant on this bill. But do not let them forget that we on this side have feelings in the same way. We feel that the bill is a good one. We do not feel that it is as bad as they make out. We feel strongly that it ought to go forward.
If I have any time tomorrow, Mr. Speaker, I shall explain my final reason.

1.	How many mines are in production in the county of Hastings?
2.	Where are they located, what are their names and what are they producing?
Answer by: Hon. George Prudham (Minister of Mines and Technical Surveys):
1.	Five.
2.	Near Marmora, Ontario-Marmoraton Mining Co. Ltd. Iron ore-operating open pit mine with beneficiation and pelletizing plant handling 4,250 tons ore per day.
Near Bancroft, Ontario-Faraday Uranium Mines Ltd. Uranium-underground operation, opening up uranium deposit and erecting 750 ton mill; expected to be in production in 1956.
Near Bancroft, Ontario-Greyhawk Uranium Mines Ltd. Uranium-the company is exploring property, and have outlined ore and have applied for a marketing contract to Eldorado Mining and Refining Ltd.
Near Madoc, Ontario-Canada Talc Industries Ltd. Talc-operating talc mine and 150 ton mill in which ore is crushed and sized for the trade.
Near Belleville, Ontario-Canada Cement Co. Ltd. Cement-quarry supplies limestone for their No. 5 plant which has a capacity
of 16 million bags per year.
